lead: Unit 4 answers two questions: how much of the energy we handle can really become work, and how do we get one property from another when we cannot measure it. After this unit you can find available and unavailable energy, do an exergy balance with second law efficiency, use the Gibbs and Helmholtz functions to test spontaneity, derive and apply the Maxwell relations, and compute saturation pressure with the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
about: Chapter 4.1 splits heat into an available part and an unavailable part and fixes the dead state. 4.2 turns that split into an exergy balance with destruction and second law efficiency. 4.3 introduces the Gibbs and Helmholtz functions, the potentials that decide whether a process can go on its own. 4.4 takes the exact differentials of those potentials and produces the Maxwell relations, so p-v-T data can supply entropy. 4.5 applies one Maxwell relation to a phase change and gives the Clausius-Clapeyron equation. Every chapter leans on the entropy of Unit 3 and the property tables of Unit 5, and none of them re-teaches those.

chapters.idea: Of heat Q taken from a source at T, only Q(1 − T₀/T) can become work with the environment at T₀; the rest, T₀ΔS, is unavailable.
chapters.depth: Dead state (environment at T₀ and p₀) defined first. Available energy A = Q(1 − T₀/T) = Q − T₀ΔS, unavailable energy = T₀ΔS, with T in kelvin. Extend to a closed system: Φ = (U − U₀) + p₀(V − V₀) − T₀(S − S₀). Show that availability depends on the dead state, so it is not a property of the system alone. Some syllabi call available energy 'availability' and unavailable energy 'anergy'. Keep to one source, one sink, no exergy balance yet.

figure.aria: Two curves that add to one: the available fraction 1 − 300/T rises with source temperature while the unavailable fraction 300/T falls.

chapters.example: Heat of 1000 kJ is supplied from a reservoir at 500 K. The environment is at 300 K. Find the available and the unavailable part of this heat. Answer: available = Q(1 − T₀/T) = 1000 × (1 − 300/500) = 400 kJ. ΔS of the reservoir = 1000/500 = 2 kJ/K, so unavailable = T₀ΔS = 300 × 2 = 600 kJ. Check: 400 + 600 = 1000 kJ.
chapters.trap: Using the actual sink temperature, or the working fluid's own temperature, in place of T₀. Also treating unavailable energy as the heat a real engine rejects: it is T₀ times the entropy change, whatever engine is used.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for entropy and reversible processes; Unit 2 for the first law of a closed system.
chapters.leave: Exergy of a flowing stream, exergy destruction and second law efficiency belong to 4.2. Entropy itself is Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Exergy is the maximum useful work a system or stream can deliver on the way to the dead state, and the part the second law destroys is T₀ times the entropy generated.
chapters.depth: Flow exergy ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀) and closed-system exergy Φ = (u − u₀) + p₀(v − v₀) − T₀(s − s₀). Exergy balance for a steady device: exergy in − exergy out − I = 0, with irreversibility (exergy destroyed) I = T₀S_gen, the Gouy-Stodola result. Second law efficiency η_II = exergy recovered ÷ exergy supplied, contrasted with isentropic efficiency so the two are not mixed. One turbine and one heat exchanger are enough. Some syllabi write 'availability' for exergy and 'irreversibility' for exergy destruction.

figure.title: Exergy balance of a steady-flow device
figure.aria: Exergy carried in by the stream leaves as useful work and stream exergy, while the difference is destroyed and equals T0 times the entropy generated.

chapters.example: Steam enters an adiabatic turbine at h₁ = 3200 kJ/kg, s₁ = 6.80 kJ/kg·K and leaves at h₂ = 2600 kJ/kg, s₂ = 7.00 kJ/kg·K. The dead state is at T₀ = 300 K. Find the work per kg, the exergy destroyed and the second law efficiency. Answer: w = h₁ − h₂ = 600 kJ/kg. S_gen = s₂ − s₁ = 0.20 kJ/kg·K, so I = T₀S_gen = 300 × 0.20 = 60 kJ/kg. Exergy drop of the stream = 600 + 60 = 660 kJ/kg. η_II = 600/660 = 0.909, about 91%.
chapters.trap: Reporting isentropic efficiency as second law efficiency, and taking exergy out minus exergy in as the work without the T₀Δs term. Do not swap T₀ for 298 K when the question states 300 K.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for the dead state and T₀ΔS; Unit 3 for entropy generation in an adiabatic device.
chapters.leave: Chemical exergy, exergy of mixtures and exergoeconomics are outside this unit. The Gibbs function in 4.3 is the same idea at constant T and p.

chapters.idea: Helmholtz and Gibbs functions are potentials whose fall marks a process that can go on its own, at constant T,V and constant T,p respectively.
chapters.depth: Definitions A = U − TS (Helmholtz function, also written F) and G = H − TS (Gibbs function). Exact differentials dA = −S dT − p dV and dG = −S dT + V dp, with natural variables (T,V) and (T,p). Spontaneity tests: dA ≤ 0 at constant T and V, dG ≤ 0 at constant T and p, equilibrium at the minimum. Meaning of the names: −ΔA is the maximum work at constant T, −ΔG the maximum non-pV work. One line that G = μn for a pure substance. Keep real-gas expansions out; only a few universities bring the Joule-Kelvin coefficient here and it is handled in 4.4.

figure.aria: U grows into H by adding pV and into A by subtracting TS, and H in turn gives G when TS is subtracted.

chapters.example: 1 kg of water freezes at 273 K and 1 atm. The latent heat of fusion is 334 kJ/kg and the volume change is negligible. Find ΔG and ΔA for the freezing. Answer: ΔH = −334 kJ and ΔS = −334/273 = −1.223 kJ/K. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −334 − 273(−1.223) = −334 + 334 = 0, as expected for a phase change at equilibrium. With ΔV ≈ 0, pΔV ≈ 0, so ΔA = ΔU − TΔS ≈ ΔH − TΔS = 0 too.
chapters.trap: Sign slips between the two differentials: dA carries −p dV and dG carries +V dp. Also quoting ΔG = 0 as a general equilibrium test when the process is at constant T and V, where A must be used.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for H = U + pV; Unit 3 for entropy as a property.
chapters.leave: Chemical potential of mixtures and phase-rule calculations go beyond this unit. The Maxwell relations taken from these differentials are 4.4.

chapters.idea: Because dU, dH, dA and dG are exact differentials, their mixed second derivatives are equal, which ties entropy to measurable pressure, volume and temperature slopes.
chapters.depth: Euler's criterion for an exact differential, applied to all four potentials, gives the four Maxwell relations: (∂T/∂V)_S = −(∂p/∂S)_V, (∂T/∂p)_S = (∂V/∂S)_p, (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂p/∂T)_V, (∂S/∂p)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_p. Derive one fully, list the other three. Uses: entropy from p-v-T data and the enthalpy relation (∂h/∂p)_T = v − T(∂v/∂T)_p. Joule-Kelvin coefficient μ = (∂T/∂p)_h = [T(∂v/∂T)_p − v]/C_p, exactly zero for an ideal gas. Only a few universities teach the van der Waals result μ ≈ (2a/RT − b)/C_p and the inversion temperature 2a/(Rb); give those in two lines.

figure.title: From an exact differential to a Maxwell relation
figure.aria: Reading the coefficients of dU as derivatives and equating the two mixed second derivatives gives one Maxwell relation; the same steps on H, A and G give the other three.

chapters.example: Air, treated as an ideal gas with R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, is compressed isothermally at 300 K from 1 bar to 5 bar. Use a Maxwell relation to find the entropy change per kg. Answer: (∂s/∂p)_T = −(∂v/∂T)_p. For an ideal gas v = RT/p, so (∂v/∂T)_p = R/p and (∂s/∂p)_T = −R/p. Then Δs = −R ln(p₂/p₁) = −0.287 × ln 5 = −0.287 × 1.609 = −0.462 kJ/kg·K.
chapters.trap: Two relations carry a minus sign and two do not; writing (∂s/∂p)_T = +(∂v/∂T)_p is the commonest error. Also fix the correct variable: the subscript is what stays constant, and it must match the potential you started from.
chapters.prereq: 4.3 for the exact differentials of A and G; Unit 3 for entropy as a property.
chapters.leave: Real-gas and Joule-Kelvin applications are optional here. The phase-change use of (∂s/∂v)_T = (∂p/∂T)_v is 4.5.

chapters.idea: Two phases in equilibrium have equal Gibbs functions, and that equality fixes the slope of the saturation line as dp/dT = h_fg/(T v_fg).
chapters.depth: Clapeyron equation dp/dT = s_fg/v_fg = h_fg/(T v_fg) for any two phases in equilibrium, derived from dG₁ = dG₂ along the boundary. Clausius-Clapeyron form for liquid-vapour, assuming ideal vapour and v_f much smaller than v_g: d(ln p)/d(1/T) = −h_fg/R, integrated to ln(p₂/p₁) = −(h_fg/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁). Uses: saturation pressure against temperature, slope of the p-T phase boundary, latent heat from vapour-pressure data, and the solid-liquid line, which for water slopes backwards because ice is less dense. Some syllabi call it simply the Clapeyron equation.

figure.aria: The saturation curve rises steeply with temperature and passes through 13.3 kPa at 323 K and 101.3 kPa at 373 K.

chapters.example: Water boils at 373 K at 101.3 kPa with h_fg = 2257 kJ/kg. Take R = 0.4615 kJ/kg·K for the vapour. Estimate the saturation pressure at 323 K. Answer: 1/T₂ − 1/T₁ = 1/323 − 1/373 = 3.0960×10⁻³ − 2.6810×10⁻³ = 4.150×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹. ln(p₂/p₁) = −(2257/0.4615)(4.150×10⁻⁴) = −4891.6 × 4.150×10⁻⁴ = −2.030. p₂ = 101.3 × e^−2.030 = 13.3 kPa. Steam tables give about 12.3 kPa; the gap comes from treating h_fg as constant.
chapters.trap: Putting Celsius into the logarithm, or mixing units so that h_fg and R are not both per kg. The integrated form is only good over a short temperature range where h_fg hardly changes; do not stretch it from 373 K down to room temperature without saying so.
chapters.prereq: 4.3 for equal Gibbs functions at phase equilibrium; 4.4 for (∂s/∂v)_T = (∂p/∂T)_v; Unit 5 for saturation data.
chapters.leave: Property values come from the steam tables of Unit 5, and the use of this curve inside the Rankine cycle is Unit 6.
